name: Opportunity Green (Giving Green, 2026)
summary: Law, policy and economics to cut emissions from aviation and shipping. A re-implementation of Giving Green's estimate of what Opportunity Green's work with climate-vulnerable countries at the International Maritime Organization (IMO), and its submission to the international law of the sea tribunal, cost per tonne of CO₂e avoided.

sections.title: From cost per tonne to tonnes per dollar
sections.explainer: charityevals' step after Giving Green's bottom line: Giving Green reports dollars per tonne; the site needs tonnes per dollar. The tonnes come from ships burning cleaner fuel in place of heavy fuel oil, so the model reports them as tonnes from burning less fuel, which the site values for the heat deaths they avoid (discounted over the decades until they come) and the air-pollution deaths they avoid at once. That is an upper bound, about 1.2 times too high on our rough guess of the smoke that goes with these tonnes (docs/normalization.md 2.5).

sections.title: Staff pay below market
sections.explainer: charityevals' step, not Giving Green's: with credit by share of resources on, staff's pay below what they could earn elsewhere counts as an in-kind contribution and gets its share of the outcome. Off by default.

rows.label: …is x times as cost-effective as the top recommendation benchmark
Tonnes of CO₂e averted per dollar
rows.explainer: One over Giving Green's cost per tonne. Reported as tonnes from burning less fuel, which count their air-pollution deaths at the shared world average (1.46 per 10,000 tonnes) as well as their heat deaths. Ship smoke is about twice that average per tonne of CO₂: Sofiev et al. (2018) estimate about 266,000 deaths a year from ship emissions after the 2020 sulphur limit (the abstract's ~250,000), from about 870 million tonnes of CO₂, some 3.1 deaths per 10,000 tonnes. But the IMO's standard lowers the greenhouse-gas intensity of ship fuel rather than how much is burned, so only part of that smoke goes with each well-to-wake tonne: liquefied gas removes sulphur and most particles while cutting well-to-wake CO₂e only 15–20%, which puts a lot of smoke on each tonne; ammonia and methanol still emit NOx; and part of each tonne is upstream fuel supply. Our rough, unsourced guess is 40% of ship smoke, about 1.2 deaths per 10,000 tonnes or 0.83 of the world average. At that guess this unit overstates the result about 1.2 times, while counting heat only would understate it about 30 times; it is the nearer of the two. Below about a quarter of ship smoke per tonne, heat only would be nearer (see the write-up).

Share of the full cost paid in cash
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, staff's forgone pay counts as part of the cost, and staff get their share of the outcome. Off, this is 100%.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted per dollar donated
rows.explainer: The tonnes per dollar above; with credit by share of resources, times the share of the full cost paid in cash (staff's forgone pay is the rest). The site turns these tonnes into years of healthy life through the deaths they avoid: "Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂", its air-pollution part at once and its heat part discounted over "Years until the heat deaths from a tonne of CO₂".
